newsitem.title: FRANCE: Seguin elected new leader of France's Gaullists.
newsitem.headline: Seguin elected new leader of France's Gaullists.

text.p: Five weeks after a disastrous election defeat, France's Gaullist RPR party on Sunday elected former National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin as its new leader, succeeding former Prime Minister Alain Juppe.
Seguin won 79 percent of the ballots cast at a special congress of the conservative Rally for the Republic party, easily defeating five rival candidates.

The congress brought together more than 4,000 party activists in search of new leadership they hope can guide them out of the political wilderness after they were unexpectedly swept from power in a June 1 parliamentary election.

The left-leaning populist Seguin, a potential rival to President Jacques Chirac, was given the reins of the party after Juppe, a longtime Seguin rival who had led the rightist government's disastrous campaign, accepted responsibility for the defeat.
Juppe had stepped down as prime minister days before the June 1 runoff in the two-round election but had initially hesitated to give up the party leadership post.
He later agreed to step down voluntarily.
But in a parting shot, he thanked the congress, five years in advance, for supporting Chirac's reelection when his current seven-year presidential term ends in 2002.
Following Seguin's victory, the congress was read a message from Chirac, who founded the RPR in 1976 to carry on the tradition of former president Charles de Gaulle.
In his message, Chirac expressed confidence in Seguin's leadership and thanked Juppe for his past service.

The RPR congress was just one part of a recomposition of the defeated right, over which the weakened president, forced to yield much of his power to a left-wing government led by Socialist Lionel Jospin, has had only limited influence.
Seguin, 54, is a heavyweight orator who led the "no" campaign in a 1992 referendum on the Maastricht treaty on European union.
He has since said he generally favours the shift to the euro single currency and greater European integration.
Seguin has put his rhetorical talent to immediate use in attacking Prime Minister Jospin but has not yet come up with a coherent political line for the new opposition.

He has also pledged allegiance to Chirac, saying the role of a renovated RPR will be to "relay and support the president's initiatives". The two men have resumed weekly lunch meetings to discuss strategy.

But Seguin has irked the head of state by cutting a deal with ex-prime minister Edouard Balladur's faction, and his associates have made clear they see him as a potential candidate to succeed Chirac when the president's term expires in 2002.

The president has spent much of the last two weeks trying to restore his influence in the party and help guide the rebuilding of the right, holding a series of individual meetings with party leaders and defeated members of parliament.
